questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a research question from a bare subject label
questions.stem: A researcher lists several possible openings for a study about adolescent sleep. Which one states a research question rather than a topic or a bare count?

options.text: Does nightly screen time predict how long adolescents sleep the next night?
Adolescent sleep
options.misconception: labels a subject area in place of a claim about a relationship

options.text: How many hours do adolescents sleep?
options.misconception: treats a bare count with no predicted relationship as a research question

options.text: What do adolescents think about sleep?
options.misconception: asks for opinions without naming any measured variables

questions.explanation: A research question names the variables to be measured and the relationship to be examined between them, and only option A does that. A topic such as adolescent sleep names a field without asserting anything, and a bare count describes a single quantity with nothing to compare it against, while an opinion question records attitudes rather than testing a relationship between measured variables.
questions.hint: Look for the entry that names two measured variables and a link between them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a testable prediction from an open research question
questions.stem: A study will compare two ways of delivering a training module to the same course. Which statement is a hypothesis rather than a research question?

options.text: In-person instruction will produce higher post-test scores than video instruction.
How does the delivery method affect post-test scores?
options.misconception: confuses an open research question with a specific testable prediction

options.text: What do learners report about the two delivery methods?
options.misconception: asks for opinions rather than stating a testable prediction

options.text: Which delivery method do instructors prefer to use?
options.misconception: asks about instructor preference rather than predicting a measured outcome

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a specific prediction that names what will be measured, in which direction the result should fall, and for which group, which is exactly what option A states. An open question such as how the method affects scores leaves the answer unspecified and can be narrowed later, while questions about what learners report or what instructors prefer gather opinions that no outcome measure would confirm or refute.
questions.hint: Ask which statement already commits to a direction and an outcome.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise a claim that data could refute
questions.stem: Four claims are proposed before data collection. Which one is falsifiable, so that some possible result would show it to be wrong?

options.text: Students given worked examples will make fewer errors on new problems.
Worked examples are pedagogically effective.
options.misconception: calls a broad endorsement falsifiable without naming an outcome

options.text: Good teaching matters a great deal in mathematics.
options.misconception: treats a value judgement as a testable prediction

options.text: Some teaching approaches are better than others.
options.misconception: leaves both approaches unspecified so nothing could count against it

questions.explanation: Falsifiability means a specified outcome could come out the other way, and option A fixes both the manipulated feature and the measured outcome, so more errors would count against it. A general endorsement has no named outcome to fail, a value judgement has no measurement attached at all, and a vague comparison leaves both sides undefined so no result can contradict it.
questions.hint: Ask which claim specifies an outcome that could come out the other way.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify an operational definition of an abstract construct
questions.stem: A study wants to measure the construct of student engagement. Which statement is an operational definition of that construct?

options.text: The count of voluntary questions a student asks during one class session.
The degree to which a student feels interested in the lesson.
options.misconception: restates the construct in other words rather than naming a procedure

options.text: How engaged students generally are in school life.
options.misconception: offers a general impression with no measurable procedure attached

options.text: A student's interest in the subject matter being taught.
options.misconception: describes a related attitude without specifying any observable count

questions.explanation: An operational definition fixes a rule for turning an abstract construct into something countable or recordable, and option A names both the behaviour to watch and the tally to keep, so two observers could follow it. The other three stay inside the construct, restating interest or engagement in fresh words without ever specifying a procedure, which means two researchers could apply them and record different numbers.
questions.hint: Ask whether two observers following the wording would record the same number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the manipulated variable in an experiment
questions.stem: Researchers vary how many practice problems students receive before a test, then record the test scores. Which variable is the independent variable in this study?

options.text: The number of practice problems, because researchers set it
The test score, because it is what the study measures
options.misconception: names the outcome variable as the one the researchers manipulate

options.text: Each student's prior ability, because it comes before the study
options.misconception: confuses a background control variable with the manipulated one because it comes earlier

options.text: The hours students spend studying at home, because it precedes the test
options.misconception: treats an uncontrolled background influence as the manipulated variable

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the researcher deliberately varies and controls, which is the number of practice problems, while the score is the dependent variable because it is what responds. Prior ability and home study hours matter to the study but they are not manipulated, and arriving earlier in time or in the causal order does not make a variable the independent one.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity the researchers decided in advance to change.

provenance.author: bank-team-resmeth
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify a third variable that varies with the treatment and the outcome
questions.stem: A coach compares vertical jump height in players who chose a new supplement with players who did not. The players who took it had also trained twice a week for a year. What is the confound?

options.text: Weekly training frequency, because it differs between the groups too
Vertical jump height, because it is the outcome being compared
options.misconception: names the dependent variable as if it were the third variable

options.text: The supplement brand, because it differs between the two groups
options.misconception: treats a property of the treatment itself as an outside influence

options.text: The length of the study, because both groups were followed over time
options.misconception: points at a feature shared by both groups rather than a between-group difference

questions.explanation: A confound is a third factor that differs between the comparison groups and tracks with the outcome, and training frequency fits because the supplement users trained more and extra training raises jump height on its own. Jump height is the dependent variable rather than a third cause, the brand is part of the treatment itself rather than an outside influence, and a study length shared by both groups cannot separate the groups at all.
questions.hint: Find the factor that differs between the groups and also affects the outcome.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state what a control condition isolates in a comparison
questions.stem: A drug trial gives one group a new sleep medication and another an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient. What does the pill with no active ingredient isolate?

options.text: The chemical effect of the drug, by holding the pill experience constant
The effect of side effects, by removing them from the treated group
options.misconception: assumes the inert pill strips side effects out of the treated group

options.text: The effect of the clinic setting, by making every visit identical
options.misconception: credits the control for holding the setting constant rather than for isolating the drug

options.text: The effect of sleep itself, by measuring it in both groups at once
options.misconception: treats the measured outcome as the thing the control isolates

questions.explanation: An inert but identical pill is matched to the treatment on everything except the active ingredient, so the two groups share the act of swallowing a tablet, the visit, and the expectation of relief, leaving the drug's chemistry as the only systematic difference. It cannot remove side effects from the treated group because the treated group takes the real drug, and keeping the setting constant is what blinding adds rather than what the pill provides.
questions.hint: Ask what the two conditions still have in common once the drug is removed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state what random assignment balances across conditions
questions.stem: Participants are assigned to study conditions by a computer-generated random sequence rather than by preference. What does that random assignment achieve?

options.text: It balances measured and unmeasured participant traits across conditions
It guarantees that the two conditions hold identical participants
options.misconception: believes random assignment produces literally identical groups rather than balance

options.text: It removes the need for a control condition in the comparison
options.misconception: thinks randomisation substitutes for having a comparison group at all

options.text: It ensures any difference found is large enough to matter in practice
options.misconception: assumes randomisation guarantees a practically important effect size

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads both the characteristics researchers thought to measure and the ones they never thought about evenly across conditions on average, so a pre-existing difference is unlikely to line up with the treatment. It is a tendency rather than a guarantee, since a particular randomisation can still land unbalanced, and it neither supplies a comparison group nor makes the resulting effect practically large.
questions.hint: Focus on the word balance, and on which traits it covers.

provenance.author: bank-team-resmeth
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the difference a placebo condition controls
questions.stem: In a trial of a new painkiller, half the patients get the drug and half get a sugar pill of identical appearance. What does the sugar pill control for?

options.text: Expectations about pain relief, which can shift reported pain
The pharmacological strength of the drug, which the pill lacks
options.misconception: confuses the control's inertness with the property it is meant to isolate

options.text: The natural course of the complaint, which both groups undergo
options.misconception: credits the inert pill with holding the untreated course constant

options.text: The side effects of the drug, which only one group receives
options.misconception: claims the inert pill removes side effects that only the drug supplies

questions.explanation: An inert pill keeps the ritual of treatment, the visit, and the belief that something is being given, so both groups can expect relief and both can report it, leaving the drug's chemistry as the only systematic difference in what the two arms experience. The pill's lack of strength is the very thing that makes it a control, and the natural course is handled by having any comparison group rather than by the pill specifically.
questions.hint: Ask what both groups would believe and feel, given that both take a pill.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the bias that double blinding removes
questions.stem: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers rating their outcomes know each participant's condition. What bias does this remove?

options.text: Expectancy effects on both sides of the measurement, from belief alone
Sampling error, which randomisation alone cannot reduce
options.misconception: thinks blinding reduces the random variation produced by sampling

options.text: Attrition, which occurs when participants leave a study early
options.misconception: assumes blinding stops people from dropping out of a study

options.text: Confounding, which random assignment balances on average
options.misconception: believes blinding is what balances participant traits across conditions

questions.explanation: Blinding cuts the channel through which knowing the assignment changes what happens: a participant who believes they got the drug may report less pain, and a rater who knows the condition may score more generously, so masking both sides removes those expectancy effects. It does nothing about the random scatter inherent in sampling, and balancing pre-existing traits is what random assignment does rather than what masking does.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when someone's belief about their own group changes their reporting.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the margin of error for a confidence interval on a proportion
questions.stem: A random survey of 625 households finds that 300 recycle weekly, a sample share of 0.48. Using a multiplier of 1.96, what is the margin of error for a 95 percent interval on the true share? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The standard error of a share is the square root of the share times its complement over the sample size, so the square root of 0.48 times 0.52 over 625 is 0.019984, and 1.96 times that is 0.0392. The counts give the same figure because 300 of 625 is 0.48, and dividing by 625 rather than by its square root would claim a margin near 0.002 that no survey of this size could deliver.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the share times its complement over n, then multiply by 1.96.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the margin of error for a confidence interval on a mean
questions.stem: A random sample of 144 daily step counts has a sample standard deviation of 12 steps. Using a multiplier of 1.96, what is the margin of error for a 95 percent interval on the mean? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.96 times the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size, and the square root of 144 is 12, so 1.96 times 12 over 12 lands exactly on 1.96 steps. Dividing by 144 instead of by its square root would report 0.163, and quoting 12 as the margin ignores the sample size altogether.
questions.hint: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size first.

provenance.author: bank-team-resmeth

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard error of a sample mean
questions.stem: A population of daily household water use has a standard deviation of 30 liters. What is the standard error of the sample mean when the sample size is 900? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The standard error divides the population spread by the square root of the sample size, and the square root of 900 is 30, so 30 over 30 gives 1 liter. Dividing by the sample size itself would report 0.033, and returning 30 would describe how spread out the population is rather than how precisely its mean has been pinned down.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the sample size, then divide the spread by it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute a survey response rate from contacts and returns
questions.stem: A questionnaire goes out to 1600 people on a professional mailing list and 384 completed forms come back. What share of the people contacted actually responded? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The response rate divides completed forms by everyone who was contacted, so 384 over 1600 is 0.24, or 24 percent of the contact list. Counting only the members judged eligible would shrink the denominator and flatter the rate, and treating 384 as a share of the whole membership would answer a question about coverage rather than about response.
questions.hint: Divide the number of completed forms by the number contacted.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute a proportional stratified allocation
questions.stem: A frame of 1000 students splits into strata of 600 freshmen, 300 sophomores, and 100 juniors. A stratified sample of 250 is allocated in proportion to stratum size. How many juniors does it contain?
questions.explanation: The junior stratum holds 100 of the 1000 frame members, so it is one tenth of the frame and one tenth of the sample, which is 25 juniors, with 150 freshmen and 75 sophomores making up the remaining 225. Splitting 250 into three equal pieces would throw away the proportionality that justified stratifying, and drawing 250 from the frame as one pool would leave the smallest stratum with whatever chance produced.
questions.hint: Take the smallest stratum's share of the frame and apply it to 250.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the size of a cluster sample
questions.stem: A district has 30 clusters of 25 students each. A cluster sample draws 8 of the 30 clusters at random and takes every student in each chosen cluster. How many students does it include?
questions.explanation: Cluster sampling keeps whole clusters intact, so 8 chosen clusters at 25 students each give 8 times 25, which is 200 students. Counting the 8 clusters themselves would report sampling units rather than people, and drawing 8 students from each of 25 clusters would be a different design that fixes the number of clusters instead of the number of people.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of chosen clusters by the students inside one cluster.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute raw agreement between two independent coders
questions.stem: Two coders working independently classify the same 40 records and agree on the category for 34 of them. What is their raw percentage agreement? Report the percent as a number.
questions.explanation: Raw agreement divides matching decisions by all decisions, so 34 out of 40 is 0.85, which is 85 percent, and the 6 records they split on are the 15 percent complement rather than an extra to add. Counting the two coders' passes separately would double the denominator to 80 and halve the apparent agreement even though the coding itself never changed.
questions.hint: Divide the number of matching classifications by the total number classified.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: determine the sample size needed to halve a margin of error
questions.stem: A survey reports a 95 percent margin of error of 4 percentage points from 500 completed responses. Holding everything else fixed, what completed sample size would cut that margin to 2 points?
questions.explanation: The margin of error falls as the square root of the sample size, so halving it takes four times as many completed responses, and 4 times 500 is 2000. Simply doubling the sample would shrink the margin by about 1.41 times, leaving it near 2.8 points, and holding the margin where it is while adding responses would buy precision the study does not need.
questions.hint: Remember the margin shrinks as the square root of n, not in step with it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of a group sitting at the top of a scale
questions.stem: On a five-point confidence scale, 40 students rate how comfortable they feel with new lab equipment and exactly 22 select the top category. What percentage of the group sits at the ceiling?
questions.explanation: A ceiling effect means ratings pile up where the scale runs out of room, and 22 of the 40 students is 0.55, so 55 percent of the group is pressed against the top. The other 18 students spread over the four lower categories, and reporting 45 percent would count the students who stayed below the top rather than those who hit it.
questions.hint: Divide the number choosing the top category by the size of the whole group.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the sample size needed for a target margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster wants a 95 percent margin of error of at most 5 percentage points on a share that could be as high as 0.50. Using a multiplier of 1.96, what is the smallest sample size that achieves this?
questions.explanation: The required size is 1.96 squared times the share times its complement over the squared margin, which is 3.8416 times 0.25 over 0.0025, giving 384.16, and a sample size must be a whole number rounded up to 385. Rounding down to 384 leaves a margin of 0.0500, just outside the target, while 385 brings it to 0.0499, just inside.
questions.hint: Rearrange the margin formula for n, then round the result upward.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the frame that supports a representative sample
questions.stem: A researcher wants a sample that represents every adult living in a region. Which group of people serves as the sampling frame for that aim?

options.text: A complete list covering every adult resident of the region
The first 500 adults who visit the central library
options.misconception: treats whoever is easiest to reach as a stand-in for the population

options.text: The adults listed in the telephone directory's society pages
options.misconception: uses a self-selected directory of joiners as if it listed the population

options.text: Every adult who is listed on a landline telephone account
options.misconception: assumes a telephone listing covers every resident, missing households without one

questions.explanation: The frame is the full list the sample is drawn from, so it has to contain the people the study is about, which is why a complete residency listing is the right starting point. Library visitors and society-page names are whoever showed up rather than a listing of residents, and a telephone listing silently drops everyone reachable only by mobile, so all three leave whole kinds of people outside the draw.
questions.hint: Ask which option lists the people the study is about, rather than the people it can find.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: select the design that guarantees representation in small subgroups
questions.stem: Results must be reported separately for three age bands, and each band holds only a small share of the population. Which sampling design best serves that need?

options.text: Stratified sampling, sorting the frame by age band before drawing
Simple random sampling, drawing every respondent from one flat list
options.misconception: assumes a flat random draw will land enough people in each small band

options.text: Cluster sampling, treating whole age bands as the units drawn
options.misconception: treats whole age bands as the units to be sampled rather than a way to separate them

options.text: Voluntary response sampling, inviting anyone willing to take part
options.misconception: expects self-selected volunteers to distribute themselves evenly across the bands

questions.explanation: Stratifying means splitting the frame into the groups the study must report on and drawing a set number from each, so every band is guaranteed representation no matter how small it is. A flat random draw can leave a small band with only a handful of people, cluster sampling would hand over whole bands and destroy the comparison, and volunteers place themselves wherever they like.
questions.hint: Ask which design guarantees a set number from each group you must report on.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state what cluster sampling gives up in exchange for convenience
questions.stem: Cluster sampling is chosen because whole groups are already on site and cheap to visit. What does that bargain cost the study?

options.text: Precision, because everyone sampled sits inside a few whole groups
Precision, because measuring a whole group beats drawing a flat sample
options.misconception: believes covering a whole group makes the sample tighter than a flat random one

options.text: Nothing, because the groups were chosen by a random procedure
options.misconception: denies any penalty on the grounds that the groups were randomly selected

options.text: Frame quality, because convenient group lists are never complete
options.misconception: reports the loss of precision as though the frame itself had failed

questions.explanation: People inside one cluster tend to resemble each other, so a sample of eight whole schools holds far less variety than eight hundred people drawn from everywhere, and that is why the margin of error grows. Random selection of the clusters keeps the choice honest but cannot create variety that was never in the sample, and the price paid is precision rather than a defective frame.
questions.hint: Think about how much variety survives when only a few groups are used.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: predict the direction a nonresponse pattern pushes an estimate
questions.stem: An income survey goes to a random sample, and only the households with above-average income tend to reply. In which direction does the reported income get pushed?

options.text: Upward, because the households that answer hold more than those that stay silent
Downward, because the households that answer are the small minority
options.misconception: assumes that fewer replies must drag the estimate downward

options.text: Nowhere, because drawing the sample at random blocks any such shift
options.misconception: believes random selection makes the pattern of replies irrelevant

options.text: Inward, because both income extremes are equally likely to answer
options.misconception: claims the middle is over-represented when the two tails answer differently

questions.explanation: When willingness to answer is tied to the thing being measured, the replies are no longer a random slice of the frame, and here the high earners are over-represented among them, so the mean lands above the truth. Counting fewer replies tells you nothing about direction, random drawing only protected who was selected rather than who chose to reply, and the two income tails are not answering alike here.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of household is over-represented among the replies.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain what a low response rate threatens in a survey
questions.stem: Only 9 percent of the people contacted returned a completed questionnaire. Why does that rate matter more than the raw count of replies?

options.text: Non-responders can differ systematically, so replies need not represent the frame
A low rate proves the wording was poor rather than the topic being sensitive
options.misconception: jumps from a low rate to one certain cause with nothing to support it

options.text: A low rate shrinks the margin of error to an unacceptably tight value
options.misconception: confuses a thinner response with a more precise estimate

options.text: Nine percent is too little to count, so no analysis can be built on it
options.misconception: treats a low but workable response as though no sample existed

questions.explanation: The danger is not the raw count but who the missing people are, because a rate this low usually means the topic turned some kinds of people away, and those people can differ from the repliers on the very variable being studied. Fewer replies also widen the margin of error rather than tightening it, and nothing in the rate alone reveals whether the wording or the subject drove people away.
questions.hint: Ask what is known about the people who did not reply.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the ratio-level variable in a set of recorded measures
questions.stem: A logbook records shoe size, satisfaction on a five-point scale, and temperature in degrees Celsius. Which of the three sits at the ratio level?

options.text: Temperature in degrees Celsius, because zero is not the absence of heat
Satisfaction on the five-point scale, because the categories are numbered
options.misconception: treats an ordered opinion scale as ratio merely because it is numbered

options.text: Shoe size, because each size stands for a real length of foot
options.misconception: assumes any numbered scale automatically carries a true zero

options.text: Satisfaction on the five-point scale, because the categories are equally spaced
options.misconception: credits equal spacing on an opinion scale with ratio-level status

questions.explanation: Ratio level requires a real zero where none of the quantity is present, and Celsius fails that test because zero degrees is water at freezing rather than no heat, so a reading of 20 is not twice a reading of 10. A satisfaction rating is ordinal at best, since the gaps between categories are not guaranteed equal and zero on such a scale means nothing, and shoe size behaves the same way.
questions.hint: Ask whether zero on the scale means none of the thing is present.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: separate consistency from accuracy in a faulty measure
questions.stem: A weighing machine reports the same number for the same bag on every reading, yet it always reads 3 kilograms high. Which description fits?

options.text: Reliable but not valid, since it repeats without being right
Valid but not reliable, since accuracy shifts from reading to reading
options.misconception: reverses the two, treating a repeating wrong number as an unstable one

options.text: Neither reliable nor valid, since a constant error ruins both
options.misconception: assumes a steady bias also destroys the consistency of the readings

options.text: Both reliable and valid, since a constant offset is easy to correct
options.misconception: credits repeatability as accuracy and writes off the bias entirely

questions.explanation: Reliability is repeatability, and validity is measuring what the scale claims to measure, and this machine is perfectly consistent while sitting 3 kilograms off the truth, so the two must be judged separately. A constant bias leaves the readings as repeatable as ever, and while it happens to be correctable, a measure cannot be called valid merely because someone has spotted a fixable error.
questions.hint: Ask separately whether the number repeats and whether the number is right.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise evidence that a measure predicts a separate outcome
questions.stem: A team reports that a new screening score predicts which trainees will later fail a performance review. Which kind of validity does that demonstrate?

options.text: Criterion validity, because the score predicts an outcome measured separately
Content validity, because the score covers the full range of job tasks
options.misconception: confuses coverage of a job's tasks with predicting an outside outcome

options.text: Construct validity, because the score measures the ability it is named for
options.misconception: confuses agreement with a theory with prediction of a separate outcome

options.text: Face validity, because trainees recognise the score as reasonable
options.misconception: relies on appearances convincing rather than on any collected evidence

questions.explanation: Criterion validity is established by checking a measure against an outside criterion already judged to be meaningful, and the performance review is exactly that, so agreement with later failure is criterion evidence. Content validity would come from showing the items cover the domain, construct validity from showing the scores behave as the theory says, and face validity from looking sensible, none of which is prediction against an outside outcome.
questions.hint: Ask whether the measure was checked against an outside criterion.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise evidence gathered from a theoretical model
questions.stem: A questionnaire is titled Job Satisfaction, and the researchers test whether its scores behave the way the underlying theory says the construct should. What are they assessing?

options.text: Construct validity, whether the scores behave as the theory predicts
Criterion validity, whether the scores predict a supervisor's rating
options.misconception: swaps the theory check for a check against an outside outcome

options.text: Content validity, whether the items cover every task in the role
options.misconception: swaps the theoretical check for a check on item coverage

options.text: Reliability, whether the same scores return on a second sitting
options.misconception: treats agreement with a theory as though it were repeatability over time

questions.learningObjective: name the reliability type matched to a repeated administration

options.text: Test-retest reliability, stability across a repeat administration
Inter-rater reliability, agreement among the judges scoring the answers
options.misconception: reads a gap between sittings as agreement between judges

options.text: Internal consistency, agreement among the items given at once
options.misconception: reads stability over time as agreement among items in one sitting

options.text: Parallel forms reliability, agreement between two worded versions
options.misconception: assumes a repeat administration is the same as a second worded version

questions.explanation: Test-retest reliability asks whether the instrument gives the same reading to the same people on a second occasion, so a two-week gap with unchanged scores is the matching design. options.misconception: blames the number of response options instead of the paired wording

options.misconception: claims feelings cannot be rated, ignoring routine use of rating scales

options.text: It asks about pay, which is confidential and cannot be measured
options.misconception: treats confidentiality of a topic as a bar to measuring it

options.misconception: treats a scale-width problem as the real defect in a leading item

options.text: An average of 4.1 is high, so the service must be working
options.misconception: reads a high average on a biased item as proof the service works

options.text: The item asks about satisfaction rather than about service quality
options.misconception: substitutes a different construct for the one the survey actually asked about

questions.learningObjective: explain how a lopsided response scale distorts answers

Three choices give more precision than an opinion can support
options.misconception: reverses the concern, treating more options as inherently more accurate

options.text: There is no middle option, so an average cannot be computed at all
options.misconception: insists on a neutral midpoint and misses the missing negative options

options.text: The options overlap in meaning, so respondents cannot tell them apart
options.misconception: blames overlapping wording for what is really a missing response

questions.explanation: Two agreeing options against one disagreeing option invites respondents to drift toward agreement, because the negative side is thin and the mildest disagreement is not offered, so the resulting average overstates how many agree. options.text: Satisfaction scores shift too much to be reported week to week
options.misconception: blames reporting stability rather than the ordering of the items

options.text: Respondents grew more generous as the study went on, nothing else
options.misconception: reads a number pattern as a drift in mood rather than as priming

questions.explanation: Having just rated the service highly, a respondent carries that rating forward and rates the next items consistently with it, so the later scores partly reflect the earlier answers rather than a fresh judgement. options.misconception: assumes pilot participants are merged into the main data set

options.misconception: believes piloting the instrument performs the main study's randomisation

options.misconception: labels a post-contact selection effect as a gap in the frame

options.text: Sampling error, because the random draw missed the right proportions
options.misconception: blames the random draw for a pattern arising after contact

options.text: Measurement error, because the questions are worded in a leading way
options.misconception: blames the wording for a pattern set by who chooses to answer

options.misconception: invents a fixed update cycle and treats the list as stale on that basis

options.misconception: treats a large frame as a weakness rather than a strength

options.text: The two items should be averaged, since averaging untangles the mixture
options.misconception: believes averaging two constructs makes the combined score interpretable

options.misconception: picks the number of opportunities rather than the measured behaviour

options.text: The number of questions a student would like to ask
options.misconception: substitutes a hypothetical intention for the recorded behaviour

options.misconception: points at a feature held constant across groups rather than one that differs

options.misconception: points at a shared feature of the design that cannot separate the arms

options.text: Criterion validity is weak, because no outside outcome is used
options.misconception: reaches for a prediction flaw when the gap is in the items themselves

questions.learningObjective: explain why more participants do not remove a built-in difference

Yes, because a large sample shrinks every systematic difference

options.text: Yes, because random scatter cancels out as participants accumulate

options.text: No, because the study now needs a control condition to be valid
options.misconception: answers with a design requirement rather than about sample size

options.text: The task is too abstract, so shoppers cannot follow the instructions
options.misconception: claims the instructions are unclear when the fault is the domain covered

options.misconception: reports the observed rate as though the scheme were thereby fixed

options.misconception: forces agreement by overwriting one of the two records

options.text: Delete the disputed records and report agreement on the rest
options.misconception: throws out exactly the cases that exposed the missing definitions

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: justify fixing a measurement rule before data collection
questions.stem: A team wants to study resilience and plans to record one self-rating on a five-point scale. Explain why a construct such as resilience needs an operational definition before any data are collected.

answer.exemplar: Resilience names a bundle of ideas at once, such as recovering after a setback, coping under pressure, and persisting, so the word itself tells nobody what to count, how often, or for how long. An operational definition fixes one rule, for example the number of setbacks a student recovered from within one term, which means every observer records the same thing and any disagreement can be traced to the world or to the rule rather than to two private meanings of the word. This is also what makes the later validity work possible, because evidence has to be aimed at a fixed target, and a self-rating with no rule attached is a measure of whatever the respondent took the word to mean.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the label covers several ideas at once, names a concrete counting rule as the operational definition, and explains that a shared rule is what lets two observers record the same quantity and what gives later validity evidence a target to hit.
questions.hint: Ask what two researchers would count differently if each took the word in their own sense.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why random assignment covers unmeasured differences too
questions.stem: One study compares teaching methods by letting each teacher keep the class they already have, and a second assigns students to teachers at random. Explain what the random assignment buys that the intact classes do not.

answer.exemplar: Intact classes arrive with the school's streaming and the teacher's own preferences already baked in, so the two classes may differ on ability, attendance, or motivation in ways nobody measured, and any outcome gap is tangled with all of them. Random assignment spreads both the recorded traits and the ones nobody thought to record across the two conditions, so a pre-existing gap shows up in some assignments and not others and cancels across them, which is the sense in which it balances rather than in the sense of producing two identical groups in any single draw. Matching participants on observed variables can imitate this for the variables it knows about, but it cannot touch the ones that were never measured.

questions.explanation: A strong response says intact classes carry pre-existing differences the study never measured, notes that random assignment spreads measured and unmeasured traits across conditions, and explains that the balance is an average over many assignments rather than a guarantee in any one of them.
questions.hint: Ask which differences nobody in the study ever wrote down.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a placebo condition and masking are both required
questions.stem: A trial gives half the volunteers a drug and half an identical capsule, and the outcome is a pain rating the volunteers give while a researcher records it. Explain why the inert capsule and the masking of assignment are each needed to separate the drug's chemical effect from everything else.

answer.exemplar: The two protections close two different channels. The inert capsule holds the ritual constant, since both arms swallow a tablet, attend a visit, and expect something to be done, so pain can fall in both groups for the same psychological reason and that shared shift cancels in the comparison, leaving the drug's chemistry as the only systematic difference. That handles the patient's side. On the researcher's side, an unmasked rater who knows who received the drug can read those reports more generously, and here the report is the measurement itself, so a rating bias is indistinguishable from a drug effect in the data. Either protection alone leaves a channel open, because a masked trial compared against no treatment still lets volunteers guess their group from what they were or were not given.

questions.explanation: A strong response names the two channels separately, explains that the inert capsule holds expectation constant for participants, explains that masking stops the rater's knowledge from colouring a self-reported outcome, and notes that removing only one of the two protections leaves the other open.
questions.hint: Ask separately about what the volunteer believes and what the researcher knows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a good allocation from a bad frame stays unrepresentative
questions.stem: A stratified sample guarantees a set number of respondents from each age band in the frame. Explain why that guarantee still does not make the sample representative of all adults.

answer.exemplar: Stratifying only subdivides whatever list it is handed, so the age proportions it reproduces are the frame's proportions and not the population's. Take a frame built from a clinic's patient register: people who already needed care are over-represented, and when that register is sorted into age bands and sampled proportionally, every band inherits the same over-representation of people with health needs, so each band is fully represented and the total is still wrong. Representation is therefore a property of the frame first and of the allocation second, which is why careful work inside a biased frame produces a confidently and systematically unrepresentative answer rather than a random one.

questions.explanation: A strong response says stratified allocation copies the frame's composition, works a concrete example where the frame over-represents a group, and concludes that coverage of the frame is what determines representativeness regardless of how carefully the sample is drawn from it.
questions.hint: Ask whether a stratified sample copies the population's proportions or the frame's.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Nonresponse and what a rate cannot show
questions.learningObjective: explain why a quoted response rate does not settle representativeness
questions.stem: A newspaper poll reaches 12000 readers and 900 reply, yet the paper prints the result as if it described all adults. Explain why printing the response rate alongside the result does not rescue the estimate.

answer.exemplar: The count of 900 answers how many people replied, while representativeness turns on who replied, and those are separate questions. At this rate there are roughly thirteen non-replies for every reply, so the missing group is far too large to treat as a random leftover, and if the people who stayed silent differ on the measured variable then the replies are a biased slice and no headcount of them corrects the direction of the skew. Drawing the sample at random protected who was contacted, not who chose to answer, so the honest repairs are a follow-up sample of non-responders to compare against the replies and an explicit statement in the write-up of who was left out.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the size of the response from the composition of the responders, notes that the non-responders are far too numerous to be random leftovers, and explains that random drawing protected who was contacted rather than who answered.
questions.hint: Ask what the count of replies says about who replied, which is a different question.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why observing a pilot can distort the pilot's own results
questions.stem: A pretest is run with ten volunteers in a room while a researcher watches and takes notes. Explain why this can leave the pilot's own results unrepresentative of what the main study will find.

answer.exemplar: The observation is doing two jobs and the second one spoils the first. The notes are exactly what the pilot is for, since they expose the items a respondent cannot parse, but being watched also makes people read more carefully and give answers they judge acceptable, so what gets recorded is the behaviour of a small number of people performing rather than the behaviour of a respondent alone. This does not make piloting worthless; it makes the distinction between what the pilot can fix and what it can only distort the point. The wording gets fixed, the reactivity cannot be observed out of existence, comprehension is better checked in a low-pressure setting, and the write-up should say that the observed respondents were not behaving typically.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies that the notes are the intended product, explains that being watched changes how respondents read and answer, and concludes that the reactivity has to be acknowledged in the write-up rather than treated as observed away.
questions.hint: Ask what the researcher gains from the notes and what the volunteer loses by being present.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence the measurement levels by what arithmetic they permit
questions.stem: The four levels of measurement differ in how much arithmetic they safely permit. Put them in order from the level that permits the least to the level that permits the most.

options.text: Nominal, where labels carry no ordering at all
Ordinal, where categories rank but their gaps are unknown
Interval, where gaps are equal but a true zero is missing
Ratio, where gaps are equal and zero means none present

questions.explanation: A nominal label only names, so nothing can be added or ordered; ordinal adds a rank but not a guaranteed equal step; interval adds equal steps so differences become meaningful; and ratio adds a true zero so all four operations, including ratios, become meaningful. Each level inherits everything the one before it allowed and adds one permission of its own.
questions.hint: Start with the level that only names things and add one permission at a time.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a randomised controlled experiment
questions.stem: A team runs a controlled trial of a new training programme with a comparison group. Put these stages in the order they are carried out.

options.text: Recruit and screen candidates against the eligibility rules
Assign eligible participants to conditions at random
Deliver the programme or its matched control to each group
Record the outcome with assessors kept unaware of assignment
Compare the groups on that outcome and report the gap

questions.explanation: Screening must come first because only eligible people belong in the trial at all, and random assignment has to follow so that the groups are formed before anyone is treated rather than selected afterwards. Delivery then puts the two conditions into effect, outcome recording happens under masking so the assessor cannot shade the result, and only after a comparable outcome exists for both groups is there something to compare and report.
questions.hint: Form the groups before treating anyone, and mask the person who records the outcome.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence instrument construction so revisions stay cheap
questions.stem: A researcher is building a survey instrument from nothing. Put these steps in the order that keeps later corrections cheap.

options.text: State the construct each item is meant to capture
Write draft items against a balanced response scale
Review the draft for bundled and leading questions
Pretest the draft with a small group and revise it
Field the finished wording to the full sample

questions.explanation: Defining the construct first stops the writer from filling an instrument with items that measure something nearby, since wording can be fixed in minutes while a wrongly chosen construct cannot be fixed at all. Drafting and then reviewing for bundled or leading items catches faults that a pilot would only reveal after the fieldwork effort, the pilot catches what reading cannot, and only the corrected version is worth putting in front of the whole sample.
questions.hint: Fix the most expensive mistake, the one about what is being measured, before the cheap ones.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence the decisions that precede drawing a sample
questions.stem: A team must produce an estimate that can stand for a whole city. Put these decisions in the order they should precede the first contact.

options.text: Fix which residents the study is about, that is the target group
Build a list that reaches every one of those residents, the frame
Choose a method that protects the small and hard-to-reach groups
Draw the sample from that list and record who was chosen
Track who declined and compare them with those who replied

questions.explanation: The target group has to be fixed before a list means anything, since a frame of commuters cannot estimate the views of all residents. The frame then has to reach that group, the method has to protect the groups most likely to be missed, the draw records who was selected so the fieldwork can be checked against the plan, and the non-response comparison comes last because nobody has declined anything until the contact is made.
questions.hint: Nothing can be sampled before the group and the list are settled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: read what a narrower interval does and does not establish
questions.stem: Two surveys of the same question report 95 percent intervals of 32 to 40 percent from 600 replies and 35 to 37 percent from 4800 replies. What does the tighter interval show?

options.text: The larger sample narrows the margin, so the estimate is more precise
The larger sample is more representative, so the estimate is more accurate
options.misconception: confuses a narrower interval with better coverage of the population

options.text: The larger sample removes bias, so it sits closer to the truth
options.misconception: credits a bigger sample with removing a systematic bias

options.text: The two estimates disagree, so neither interval can be trusted
options.misconception: reads a difference in width as a contradiction between studies

questions.explanation: Both intervals are consistent with each other, and the narrower one reflects eight times as many replies, since the margin shrinks as the square root of the sample size. That is a gain in precision, which says how tightly this sample pins the estimate, while accuracy depends on whether the sample represented the population and nothing here establishes that. The intervals overlapping rather than conflicting is exactly what a shared truth would produce.
questions.hint: Ask what the width of an interval is a claim about, and about what it is not.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: judge a reported mean against the shape of its distribution
questions.stem: On a five-point scale, 22 percent of responses land on the top category, 38 percent on the bottom, and the middle holds a thin spread, with a mean of 3.9 reported out of 5. What is the concern?

options.text: Both ends are crowded, so a high mean flatters the middle
Both ends are crowded, so the data must be a symmetric bell shape
options.misconception: reads two crowded ends as evidence of a bell-shaped curve

options.text: The spread is too wide, so the sample must be careless
options.misconception: blames the sampling for a pattern the response scale produced

options.text: The mean is fine, since an average ignores crowding at the ends
options.misconception: believes an average is immune to the shape behind it

questions.explanation: With more than a third of responses at the bottom and nearly a quarter at the top, the middle is empty, so a single average of 3.9 describes no actual respondent and is held up by a minority at the ceiling. Two crowded ends with a hollow centre are the opposite of a bell shape, the pattern comes from how the scale was answered rather than from carelessness in sampling, and an average cannot look past the distribution that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask which respondents the reported average actually describes.
